summary: For 10-11 year-olds, this builds formal, multi-step mathematical argument and its critique half: constructing proofs by chaining facts (not measuring), finding and explaining errors in a peer's working, and the signature move of disproving a false 'always' conjecture with a single counter-example. Learners meet the proof asymmetry — one honest counter-example kills a universal claim, while confirming examples cannot establish it unless every possible case is checked (impossible for claims about all numbers) — and the logic of implication, including the claim/converse distinction. Activities span fractions, ratio, algebra and geometry, with a live adversarial dialogue as the primary vehicle and a manipulable conjecture/proof workspace, static critique cards, and a recognition warm-up as complementary alternatives serving different purposes.
misconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes bigger / division always makes smaller' — the whole-number generalisation that fails for factors below 1
Confirming a conjecture with examples and calling it proved (empirical proof scheme)
Confusing a statement with its converse ('if square then 4 right angles' ⇒ 'if 4 right angles then square')
Inverting the wrong fraction in division, or 'dividing straight across', and critiquing only by the odd-looking answer rather than the faulty step
Believing a proved geometric result holds only for the specific diagram drawn

activities.title: The confident conjecture champion (adversarial dialogue)
steps: Face an in-role character who asserts a universal claim with total confidence: 'Multiplying ALWAYS makes a number bigger — I've tried 3×4, 5×6, 10×10, works every time. So it's proved, right?'
Decide whether piling up more agreeing examples settles it, or whether you must HUNT for a case that breaks the claim.
Produce and state a decisive counter-example, e.g. '6 times a half is three — that's smaller, so it's not always,' and explain why that single case is enough.

When the champion patches the claim ('okay, multiplying always makes bigger OR the same') test the patch again: × 1/2 still shrinks it (so it breaks the patch), while × 1 only reaches the 'same' boundary the patch now allows.

When the champion defends a flawed fraction division ('just flip the FIRST fraction') locate the faulty step, say why it fails, and give the correct method (invert the divisor — the second fraction — then multiply).
Answer the champion's probes: 'Is that a proof or just examples?' and 'Does the opposite — the converse — also hold?'
activities.insight: A universal claim is destroyed by one honest counter-example, while confirming cases cannot prove it unless every possible case is checked (impossible for claims about all numbers); constructing arguments and critiquing flawed ones are the same reasoning practice, and a claim is not the same as its converse.

activities.title: Conjecture-testing and proof-building workspace
steps: Sort 'always / sometimes / never' claims and use a counter-example finder: drag values and watch a claim collapse when, say, × 1/2 makes the product shrink. Use claims whose truth value is determinate — e.g. 'multiplying makes bigger' (an 'always' claim broken by a factor below 1 such as × 1/2). If including 'the more sides a shape has, the bigger its angles', state inside the task which angle is meant (e.g. each interior angle): for regular polygons each interior angle does grow with the number of sides, but it fails for irregular shapes, so it sorts as 'sometimes' — do not present it as a straightforwardly false 'always' claim.

Build an angle-fact proof chain: snap facts ('angles on a line sum to 180°', 'angles in a triangle sum to 180°', 'vertically opposite angles are equal') into an if/therefore track to reach a proved angle such as 60°, reserving measuring only to check — and only when the chosen givens genuinely force that value.
Critique a peer's fraction division: tap the mis-inverted step and select the correct method, then state in your own words why the flawed step fails.
activities.insight: Chaining established facts yields a proved value that holds generally, not just for the drawn diagram; a well-chosen single case breaks an 'always' claim; and locating a faulty step is more productive than rejecting an answer for looking odd.

activities.title: Annotated sound-vs-flawed proofs and conjecture cards
steps: Compare an annotated correct fraction division with a flawed one side by side, and discuss where and why the flawed one goes wrong (it inverts the first fraction rather than the divisor).
Work through a set of true/false conjecture cards; tap a card to reveal either a counter-example that breaks it or a short proof sketch that supports it.
Use these as a springboard for talk: say aloud whether each revealed case is a proof or just an example, and whether the converse of a true claim also holds.
activities.insight: Seeing a flawed step laid out beside a correct one, and cards that reveal breakers or sketches, can seed critique vocabulary and prime the claim/converse distinction before learners construct their own arguments.

activities.title: Pick-the-breaker warm-up
steps: From several candidate cases, pick the one that disproves a stated 'always' claim (e.g. which case breaks 'multiplying makes bigger'?).
After choosing, say aloud why that case is decisive and why the other candidates do not break the claim.
activities.insight: Recognising which case is a counter-example is a useful entry step, but choosing from options does not itself elicit a constructed proof or a flaw explained in one's own words.

checkQuestion: A classmate is sure of this rule: 'When you multiply two numbers, the answer is always bigger than both of them — I've tried loads and it always works.' Are they right? Talk me through how you'd decide, and if you think the rule is wrong, show me the most convincing way to prove it's wrong.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child producing a counter-example with a factor less than 1 (e.g. 6 × 1/2 = 3, or 8 × 0 = 0) AND recognising that ONE such case is enough to disprove the 'always' claim, rather than adding more confirming examples or hedging.
